title: Tom Cruise Says AI Is ‘Coming and It’s Going to Happen,’ but ‘People Want to See Real Things’: ‘Keep Creating’
description:
Despite the threat of AI to the film industry, Tom Cruise is confident that people will always “want to see real things” on screen.

	At an intimate
body:
Despite the threat of AI to the film industry, Tom Cruise is confident that people will always “want to see real things” on screen.

	At an intimate BAFTA “Life in Pictures” conversation in London on Monday night, Cruise looked back on his four-decade career including acclaimed roles in “Top Gun,” “Jerry Maguire,” “Magnolia” and the “Mission: Impossible” franchise as well as to the future with his upcoming movie “Digger.” 


	On the topic of how the “Mission: Impossible” films have been at the forefront of new technology — with 2025’s “The Final Reckoning” even taking on AI as its villain — moderator Edith Bowman asked Cruise for his take on how it will impact the industry. 
	

	“Here’s the thing: There is nothing like human,” Cruise began, explaining that one of the reasons he is so bullish on keeping the theatrical experience alive is because it brings people together. 

	“I have nothing against streaming or anything like that,” he continued, saying that seeing a film in theaters is simply “a different art form.”

	He pointed to this summer’s box office — which broke all-time industry records by grossing $4.76 billion from May 1 to Labor Day — as an example of the enduring desire for human stories and craftsmanship.

	“People want that experience. They’re going to movie theaters,” Cruise said, adding: “I always believe in humanity.”

	Cruise concluded that in the face of AI, creatives must “keep creating.” 

	“You know, it is coming and it’s going to happen,” Cruise said of AI. “But people want to see real things.”

	The movie star also teased “Digger,” directed by “The Revenant” helmer Alejandro G. Iñárritu, in which he plays a wealthy oil tycoon. Cruise looks nearly unrecognizable in the role, sporting a fat suit and prosthetics he said initially took six hours to apply. 
	

	“I’ve never read a movie like this,” Cruise said. “It’s the most original film and one of the most moving films I’ve ever seen.”

	“Digger” hits theaters on Oct. 2 via Warner Bros.

schema.headline: Tom Cruise Says AI Is ‘Coming and It’s Going to Happen,’ but ‘People Want to See Real Things’: ‘Keep Creating’

title: ‘Daredevil: Born Again’ Ending With Season 3
description:
Daredevil is hanging up his mask after three seasons on Disney+.

	Marvel’s “Daredevil: Born Again,” starring Charlie Cox as the blind lawyer-turned
body:
Daredevil is hanging up his mask after three seasons on Disney+.

	Marvel’s “Daredevil: Born Again,” starring Charlie Cox as the blind lawyer-turned-vigilante, is ending with the upcoming Season 3, Variety has confirmed. The third and final season wrapped production a couple of months ago and is expected to premiere on Disney+ in 2027. Co-creator and showrunner Dario Scardapane has also exited the series, which is in the midst of post-production.
	

	Cox originally debuted as the blind hero on Netflix’s “Daredevil,” which ran for three seasons from 2015-2018 and kicked off the mini, street-level Marvel universe on the streamer. It spawned “Jessica Jones”, “Luke Cage” and “Iron Fist” spinoffs and culminated with the team-up series “The Defenders.” Disney+ revived the show as “Daredevil: Born Again” in 2025 and brought back several of the main cast members, including Vincent D’Onofrio as Wilson Fisk, aka the Kingpin of New York City, Deborah Ann Woll as Karen Page, Elden Henson as Foggy Nelson and Wilson Bethel as Bullseye.


	“Born Again” Season 2 started reuniting Netflix’s “Defenders” cast by bringing back Krysten Ritter as the super-strong private detective Jessica Jones in a supporting role, plus Mike Colter had a cameo in the finale as her lover Luke Cage. Paparazzi photos also leaked during Season 3 production, showing Finn Jones back as Danny Rand, aka the martial arts expert Iron Fist, alongside Ritter and Colter. They’re expected to team up once again to take down Kingpin, who’s been stripped of his title as New York City mayor. Meanwhile, Daredevil has found himself in jail, and his identity was made public in the wake of the Season 2 finale.
	

	Hollywood Reporter first reported the news of the series ending.

title: Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’
description: Christina Applegate has shared a first look at her life outside the hospital following a months-long stay amid her ongoing battle with multiple scle
body:
Christina Applegate has shared a first look at her life outside the hospital following a months-long stay amid her ongoing battle with multiple sclerosis.

	In the video, shared on Applegate’s Instagram account, the “Married… with Children” star is seen showing off her blonde hair while wearing a black zip-up hoodie. “Fresh hair color, new weird spot on my cheek haha thank you @davestanwell for brightening up my cloudy day,” Applegate wrote.
	

	The Emmy winner also shouted out those who have been supporting her: “Love you and love to you all out there,” she wrote.


	News first broke that Applegate had been hospitalized back in March, though the next month, she took to Instagram to share that she’d been “getting stronger and better every day.”

	“Thank you for the outpouring of love and well wishes,” she wrote in her caption on Monday. “Health issues are a constant for me, but I’m a strong chick and I’m getting stronger and better every day. I’m taking a moment to focus on my health, but I’ll be back with more to say soon enough.”

	Applegate first announced her MS diagnosis in Aug. 2021, and made her first public appearance when she attended her Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony the following year.

	When she took the stage during the ceremony, the “Dead to Me” actor began to cry when talking about her daughter.

	“The most important person in this world is my daughter,” Applegate said. “You are so much more than even you know. You are so beautiful and kind and smart and interesting. I’m blessed every day that I get to wake up and take you to school…thank you for standing by me through all of this.”
	

	Speaking to the audience, Applegate added, “Every single one of you. I love you [all] so much.”

schema.headline: Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’

title: What’s in the Paramount Settlement With States: Commitment to Not Sell Studio Lots, Additional $300M Yearly Investment in U.S. Film Production, CNN Oversight and More
description: The details of Paramount’s deal with 12 states settling their antitrust case — paving the way for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the bigges
body:
The details of Paramount’s deal with 12 states settling their antitrust case — paving the way for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, the biggest merger in Hollywood history — have been revealed.

	Among the top-line items: Paramount is agreeing to keep its operations in California and has committed to not sell the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in the state for at least five years. That comes after Paramount Skydance chief David Ellison had threatened to pull up stakes from the Golden State if he couldn’t close the WBD deal by Oct. 1.
	

	Under the terms of the proposed settlement, Paramount will invest at least an additional $300 million on film production in the U.S. annually — for a total of $1.5 billion over five years — and is obligated to release at least 30 movies for theatrical distribution per year (something Ellison has repeatedly promised he would do).


	The company also has agreed to have a third-party entity — a “news editorial independence board” — oversee news operations of CNN and CBS News, a measure intended to maintain their editorial independence under Paramount’s ownership.

	The terms of the settlement would conclude at the end of the fifth calendar year that follows the closing, so if the Paramount-WBD merger closes before the end of this year as expected, the commitment period would run through Dec. 31, 2031.

	David Ellison said in a statement: “We are grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, as well as the WGA, for engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution that serves all parties, and to Governor Newsom for his support throughout this process. Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and — most importantly — the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling. We’re confident this agreement does exactly that, memorializing a series of commitments that include 30+ films annually and expanded U.S. film production to help revitalize our industry here at home.”
	

	The merged Paramount-Warner Bros. will face penalties if it doesn’t meet those requirements, including potential divestiture of assets. The text of the proposed settlement with the states, which requires approval by the judge overseeing the case, is available at this link.

	Also Monday, the Writers Guild of America announced a settlement with Paramount resolving the WGA’s antitrust suit over the Warner Bros. merger. Under that agreement, WGA obtained a concession from Paramount “to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years.”

	Here are the key points from the Paramount settlement with the state AGs, which came after a marathon weekend of negotiations between the two sides:

	Movie commitments: Paramount-Warner Bros. is required to release minimum numbers of annual film releases in both the wide release and “tentpole” categories, among others; spend at least $300 million more annually on film production in the United States than was spent in 2025; and agree to commitments regarding pricing to theaters. In years one and two, at least 20 of a total 30 movies must be “wide release films”; that goes up to 21 of 32 movies for years 3-5. At least four of the films must be “independent films,” and at least 50% of the movies must be produced or jointly produced with another company. The merged company is required to operate a fund for purchasing indie films and make an annual contribution of $5 million per year, for a total of $25 million over five years. If the company doesn’t meet those obligations, after a six-month grace period it would be forced to divest its entire ownership interest in Miramax Studios. Also, for each film by which the merged Paramount-WB falls below the agreed thresholds, it must contribute $30 million to health care and retirement trust funds for the WGA, IATSE, DGA, International Brotherhood of Teamsters (and other unions that work on film productions) as well as the Motion Pictures & Television Fund (MPTF) — and the National Association of Attorneys General Fund.

	Theatrical windows: Paramount-Warner Bros. wide release films must have a 45-day theatrical distribution period (as Ellison had already pledge), and the company is prohibited from releasing those movies on any subscription streaming platform including Paramount+ sooner than 90 days after they premiere in theaters.
	

	Basic cable commitments: The merged company is required to conduct separate negotiations for the distribution of basic cable channels owned by Paramount and Warner Bros. for five years. The settlement puts restrictions on changes to affiliate fee negotiations and agreements with distributors, as well as a restriction on the use of confidential information of either Paramount or Warner Bros. in the negotiations of affiliate fees for the other. If the company does not uphold those commitments, it will be required to divest the following channels: BET, BET Gospel, BET Her, BET Hip-Hop, BET Jams, and BET Soul; VH1; Comedy Central; Smithsonian; Destination America; and Science,

	Maintaining both WB and Paramount lots: The company must maintain the production lots of both Paramount (5555 Melrose Ave. in Los Angeles) and Warner Bros. (4000 Warner Blvd. in Burbank, California) through at least the end of 2031.

	Employment commitments: The company must honor collective bargaining agreements and commit $47.5 million to a “workforce fund” over five years for training and career development for employees who are laid off as a result of the merger.

	News oversight board: The new Paramount-WB must form a “News Editorial Independence Board” to establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels.” The proposed settlement requires both an internal “compliance monitor” and an independent “monitoring trustee” to ensure the merged company’s compliance with the terms. In addition, a “State Committee” of five states will also oversee enforcement and monitor compliance.

	Pluto TV must stay free: At least through five-year commitment period, Paramount must continue to offer Pluto TV, its free, ad-supported streaming service, at no cost and “with service and quality levels at or above” it provides currently.

	Payment of states’ legal fees: The company will reimburse the 12 states for “reasonable attorneys’ fees and reasonable economic expert fees” they have incurred in an amount of not more than $40 million.

schema.headline: What’s in the Paramount Settlement With States: Commitment to Not Sell Studio Lots, Additional $300M Yearly Investment in U.S. Film Production, CNN Oversight and More

title: WGA Settles Antitrust Lawsuit With Paramount Over Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
description: The Writers Guild of America East and Writers Guild of America West, jointly the WGA, have settled their lawsuit to block the proposed merger of Par
body:
The Writers Guild of America East and Writers Guild of America West, jointly the WGA, have settled their lawsuit to block the proposed merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery per a statement released by the organization Monday.

	The settlement comes following the news that Paramount has reached a deal with 12 state attorneys general, removing a major obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.


	“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large. Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial,” reads the statement.
	

	The WGA also noted that while they “were not successful in blocking the merger,” the organization’s “advocacy brought more attention to the harms that this merger—and others like it—will cause. We will continue to fight the harms of industry consolidation.”

	The WGA filed the lawsuit to block the proposed $111 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance back in July. At the time, the organization alleged it would violate federal antitrust law and would cause specific harm to writers.

	“With fewer competitors, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity would have both the incentive and the ability to lower costs by suppressing writers’ wages and reducing output. Writers will be paid less and have fewer employment opportunities,” the WGA complaint stated.
	

	The WGA’s lawsuit was filed following a prior antitrust lawsuit by 12 Democratic state attorneys that same month, which similarly alleged that the merger would give Paramount-WBD anticompetitive power in theatrical and basic cable TV markets.

	Read the WGA’s full statement here:

	“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large. Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial. Consequently, we have also settled our lawsuit with an agreement from Paramount to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys’ fees in the litigation.

	Though we were not successful in blocking the merger, our advocacy brought more attention to the harms that this merger—and others like it—will cause. We will continue to fight the harms of industry consolidation.

	As the number of outlets to sell our work to and the corresponding diversity of programming shrinks, we need industry-wide structural separation between streamers and studios in order to promote competition in programming, like the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules once required in broadcast television. We will continue to fight for these goals.”

schema.headline: WGA Settles Antitrust Lawsuit With Paramount Over Warner Bros. Discovery Merger

title: David Ellison Says Paramount Hopes to Close Warner Bros. Deal in ‘Approximately Two Weeks’; Studios to Remain in California
description: Update: David Ellison isn’t looking for greener pastures. The CEO of Paramount Skydance (soon to include Warner Bros. Discovery) issued an official
body:
Update: David Ellison isn’t looking for greener pastures. The CEO of Paramount Skydance (soon to include Warner Bros. Discovery) issued an official statement that both content studios will remain in California. 

	“Now that we reached and announced a settlement, we’re eager to get to work building a stronger Hollywood. Let me be clear: the newly merged company will be headquartered in Los Angeles,” Ellison said hours after reaching a settlement with 12 state attorneys general and the WGA to clear a path for his merger.
	

	“We aren’t going anywhere. Our history is here and this is where our future is being built,” concluded Ellison. 


	Previously … 

	David Ellison’s endgame is in sight. Following a dramatic weekend of negotiations with a collection of state attorneys general and the WGA, the mogul’s path to combining Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery is now clear.

	In a Monday address to staff, Ellison said his team’s goal is to “close in approximately two weeks. That said, closing is really just the starting line. Bringing two companies this size together takes time, and we’ll share information as it becomes available.”

	The mood is celebratory on the Paramount lot, insiders said, despite the fact that much of Hollywood is observing Yom Kippur (the most reverent of the Jewish High Holy Days). One source joked that several of Ellison’s top lieutenants will be making “guilt donations” to select charities for working through the day.

	While brief, the memo focused on the combined power that “ParaBros” will now wield to provide jobs and increase content volume (a stark narrative shift from the previously opposed group of AGs, who said the merger would be anticompetitive).
	

	“This is an exciting moment for our company and our industry. If you’re like me, you’re in this business because you love the art of visual storytelling – the chance to entertain, unite and inspire the world through extraordinary stories,” added Ellison. “Together, Paramount and WBD can do more of that, for audiences everywhere. And we can’t wait to get started.” 

	Read Ellison’s full memo to staff: 

	Team,Just a few moments ago, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, on behalf of himself and 11 other State AGs, announced a settlement that clears the path forward on the lawsuit blocking our merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. We have also reached a settlement with the Writers Guild of America.With both groups’ concerns now addressed, we have complete clearance for this merger and can move toward closing. There’s still work ahead to get this deal across the finish line, but we’re excited to bring these two iconic companies together, as it means more opportunity for our creatives, production crews and employees across the business, and more great entertainment for audiences everywhere.We’re grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, and to the WGA, for engaging in good faith to reach this resolution. The agreement includes a number of commitments, including 30+ films annually and expanded U.S. film production – meant to help revitalize our industry and support the people behind it, here at home. Since we launched this bid, our goal has been to build a stronger Hollywood: more stories told, greater choice for consumers, stronger competition. Combining these companies gives us the opportunity to do just that.This is an exciting moment for our company and our industry. If you’re like me, you’re in this business because you love the art of visual storytelling – the chance to entertain, unite and inspire the world through extraordinary stories. Together, Paramount and WBD can do more of that, for audiences everywhere. And we can’t wait to get started.I know you have questions about what happens next – your role, your team and how we will work day to day. We don’t have all the answers yet, and I won’t pretend otherwise. We are tentatively planning to close in approximately two weeks. That said, closing is really just the starting line. Bringing two companies this size together takes time, and we’ll share information as it becomes available. In the meantime, if you have questions or concerns, please visit the Integration Hub, reach out to your manager or HR representative, or email internalcomms@paramount.com.Thank you for your patience, commitment and hard work throughout this process. I know it’s created real uncertainty, and for some of you, real anxiety – that’s not lost on me. Our people are what make this company one of the best in the world, and I’m truly grateful for your dedication and support. I’m confident we’re going to build something special together in the years ahead.Let’s go!David

schema.headline: David Ellison Says Paramount Hopes to Close Warner Bros. Deal in ‘Approximately Two Weeks’; Studios to Remain in California

title: Rob Bonta, Facing Skeptics, Defends ‘Very Strong’ Paramount Deal
description: Rob Bonta defended the antitrust settlement that allows Paramount to merge with Warner Bros. on Monday, saying in a 45-minute press conference that
body:
Rob Bonta defended the antitrust settlement that allows Paramount to merge with Warner Bros. on Monday, saying in a 45-minute press conference that the deal includes independent monitoring and will result in more jobs in Hollywood.

	But the deal does not include the three words — robust structural remedies — that California’s attorney general had said was the goal since filing suit in July. And while he went to some lengths to argue that the deal represents a “strong” outcome, he also acknowledged it was not his preferred result.
	

	“I don’t think these two companies should merge,” he said. “But that’s not something that we are focused on with our resolution here.”


	Bonta had come under increasing pressure in the last few weeks, as Gov. Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra, the cinema trade group, and labor leaders all expressed hope for a settlement. Paramount also did its best to increase the leverage on Bonta, threatening to relocate to Tennessee and seeking a court order to force the 12-state coalition to pay $1.88 billion for delaying the deal.

	In the press conference, Bonta sought to downplay that pressure. “That’s not what I’m thinking about, that’s not my focus,” he said. making the case that the A.G.’s victories in court put pressure on Paramount to offer significant concessions.

	“We got the antitrust resolution that we wanted,” he said. “Very strong remedies and commitments to address the concerns that we raised.”

	As to whether he thought the states could have prevailed at trial next spring, he said that courtrooms “always have risk.” He also acknowledged concerns that prolonging the case would create “uncertainty” in Hollywood, an issue that had been raised by Paramount and some labor unions.
	

	“This deal gives certainty about the future of production right here in L.A.,” he said, noting that Paramount had committed to increasing domestic production and to not selling its L.A. lots for at least five years. “That also generates important certainty for this industry that I think is craving it.”

	He also argued that the outcome is dramatically different from the Hollywood’s last major merger, the Disney-Fox deal, which went unchallenged by antitrust authorities and led to reduced production.

	“This agreement is the opposite of Disney-Fox,” he said. “The things that we saw in the Disney-Fox merger — a massive decrease in film production… this doesn’t just guard against that and protect against the downside; it locks in a massive upside.”

	Bonta was alone at the podium, without his trial team or representatives from the other 11 states involved in the suit. He was also not joined by the Writers Guild of America, which filed its own antitrust suit and also resolved it over the weekend.

	In a statement, the WGA said that the settlement terms “fall far short of adequately protecting writers,” but that it could not bear the cost of continuing its suit without support from the states.

	William Tong, the attorney general of Connecticut, also expressed dismay that the deal does not include divesture of CBS and CNN, which he said was needed to save “ethical and independent journalism.”

	“We fought aggressively for that remedy,” he said. “I am deeply disappointed that we could not do more.”

	Bonta noted that all 12 states signed on to the settlement. He also said the WGA was not involved in the states’ negotiations.

	“They brought their own case,” he said. “They decided whether or not they wanted to resolve their case and under what terms.”

	Bonta said there was no key moment or provision that unlocked the deal, and struggled to offer a timeline of how the agreement came together.

	“These days have blurred because we’ve been in some deep and robust conversations,” he said.

schema.headline: Rob Bonta, Facing Skeptics, Defends ‘Very Strong’ Paramount Deal

title: Taylor Frankie Paul Steps Away From ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ After Allegedly Failing Court-Ordered Drug Test, Citing ‘Disgusting’ Bullying From Castmates
description: Though Taylor Frankie Paul had just set her return to “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” she says she has decided to step away from the Hulu realit
body:
Though Taylor Frankie Paul had just set her return to “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” she says she has decided to step away from the Hulu reality show after the latest development in her months-long legal scandal with the fathers of her children.

	In a post on Instagram on Monday, Paul wrote that her “gratitude goes out to all the networks that supported me throughout this and gave me the chance to return. However I don’t desire to move forward like this.” She then lashed out at her “Mormon Wives” castmates, saying they’d engaged in a “pile on” — she wrote that “laughing about my kids is disgusting.” Since Season 5 of the show premiered on Sept. 10, the “Mormon Wives” cast, which has been filming Season 6 without Paul since July, have been going back and forth ceaselessly on social media.
	

	Sources told Variety last week that, as reported by TMZ, Paul allegedly failed a recent drug test ordered by a Utah court during her ongoing custody battles with her ex-boyfriend, Dakota Mortensen, which whom she shares one son, and her ex-husband, Tate Paul, with whom she shares a son and daughter. Whether Disney and Hulu would have moved forward with Paul after the failed drug test is now a question that will never be answered.


	Paul did not address the drug test allegations in her Instagram post. Neither Hulu nor representatives for Paul immediately responded to a request for comment.

	Paul was required to take the drug test after a court ruling in July, but her results were put under a protective order, preventing them from being shared outside of those directly involved in the case. Her ex-husband filed documents asking the court to unseal the results on Aug. 13, but they were not public until TMZ’s reporting.
	

	Both custody battles began after an explosion in Paul and Mortensen’s relationship back in March, when production on “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” paused due to a police investigation into domestic violence allegations the two made against each other. Soon after, TMZ published video from a separate incident between them, which showed Paul in a violent altercation with Mortensen and throwing a chair while one of her children was nearby. That prompted Disney to unschedule the premiere of “The Bachelorette” Season 22, which featured Paul as the star. With additional allegations made by both Paul and Mortensen, a court granted them mutual restraining orders, but neither of them faced charges.

	The scandal has ricocheted onto all involved with “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives,” with several online feuds occurring among cast members in the months leading up to the Sept. 10 release of Season 5. Shortly after Season 5 was released, Mikayla Matthews announced she had left the show midway through filming Season 6. She later clarified that she was leaving because of a moral objection to Paul’s return. (To that end, Paul wrote on Monday, “I originally was willing to be removed to let them all continue on with less stress and I’m back to that point.”) Cast members Mayci Neeley and Layla Taylor both indicated they were also unsure about their futures on the show after the news. Whitney Leavitt had already announced her decision to leave the show months ago, citing her budding acting career.

	Paul’s post on Monday concluded with this bit, directed toward her former #MomTok sorority: “I treated production and crew with respect always, in fact they are ones who checked on me throughout this. I agree it’s to the point of bullying for months now. What makes it harder to take in is some of these parents have made mistakes that would result in the same judgement I’m receiving yet pointing a finger. However it’s a pleasure to remove myself so they can continue, because I’ve almost convinced myself I’m deserving of all this pain and to a certain degree absolutely this is consequences of my actions. My question has been how much suffering and scrutiny is going to be enough…I’m just relieved to be out.”

schema.headline: Taylor Frankie Paul Steps Away From ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ After Allegedly Failing Court-Ordered Drug Test, Citing ‘Disgusting’ Bullying From Castmates

title: Neil Jordan on Restoring ‘Interview With the Vampire’ for 4K and Why the Film Didn’t Have Jump Scares
description: Thirty-plus years after its original release, Neil Jordan’s Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise starring gothic vampire movie “Interview with the Vampire” is a
body:
Thirty-plus years after its original release, Neil Jordan’s Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise starring gothic vampire movie “Interview with the Vampire” is available in 4K and on 4K UHD Blu-ray.

	The bonus features include never-before-seen deleted scenes, as well as two special features: “Eternal Night and Deadly Light,” where Jordan and film editor Mick Audsley discuss the approach to cinematography and the gothic romanticism achieved by director of photography Philippe Rousselot. Another feature, “Interview with the Vampire: Creating the World,” with Jordan and production designer Dante Ferretti showcases the detailed sets, augmented locations and costumes of the film.
	

	Marking the film’s release in 4K, Jordan spoke with Variety about the release, the deleted scenes and whether he’d ever consider shooting for Imax.
	
		It’s been 32 years since the film’s release. What does it mean to finally have the film in 4K?	

	We can restore the movie to the way we originally shot it. The last time I saw the film was on the 25th anniversary. I asked Warner Bros. for a 35mm print. But either the cinema or the projector lights were so low, or the print had been so degraded or something, it was so dark I couldn’t see the film. So to be able to restore it, and to scan it frame by frame, is just a wonderful opportunity. I’m glad it exists so you can basically bring a movie to life again and remind yourself why you shot it in the first place.
	
		We have to talk about the deleted scenes, like the moment with Louis in the church and inside the confessional as the priest is telling him about the capacity to forgive…	

	Why is that not in the finished movie? I don’t know. I swear to God, I was looking at it with Mick Audsley, the editor and I was saying, “Why did we not include that? It’s dramatic. it’s bloody, it’s tortured — it’s everything the movie is. Maybe it was for reasons of length. Or maybe the character Louis — his sense of suffering and his declarations of suffering — were all becoming a bit too much.
	
	
		This film has had a lasting impact, and then there was the TV show. Why do you think “Interview With the Vampire” has such lasting appeal?	

	Anne Rice changed the perception of this thing that doesn’t exist. She took the story of Bram Stoker’s “Dracula,” that image of Dracula and of the vampire. She placed it in the 18th and 19th centuries. She set it in this glamorous French Louisiana background and made the question of eternity the focus. What would it be like if you were given the gift of eternal life? What would it be like to live forever? How bored would you get with your partner — be it Tom Cruise, Brad Pitt or Kirsten Dunst? Most people can’t survive a marriage. How would you survive eternity with somebody else? She retouched the archetype of a vampire. It affected everything. It definitely affected the “Twilight” novels. In some ways, it made them far too cutesy and Heathcliffian in a way. But Anne’s stuff is still dangerous, and it deserves to be continually explored.
	
		How did you keep that danger in the film?	

	I saw it as a film about a doomed family. That’s what I thought was the center of it. That’s why I thought the part of Claudia is so important. In the book, she’s about six, or a bit younger. When she was 11 or 12, she still was a child. If you go to 14 or 15, you’re talking about a different kind of period of development. To me, it was a story about two men who are obsessed with each other. One tries to leave, and the other says, “OK.” He creates the child from the two of them. They’re stuck with each other, and she’s stuck with them and she doesn’t know why she became this thing.
	
		That, to me, was a fascinating story and that was a story that would sustain an entire movie.	

	The problem with it was I found, is that because we’re telling a story from the heart, from the perspective of the monster — from Louis’s perspective, and also from Lestat’s perspective in a way — the studio kept saying to me, “Oh, is it scary?” I had to say to them, “Look, you’re not going to get jump scares out of this because these people — you can’t kill them. You can harm them, you can burn them or expose them to daylight. But you can’t even chop off their heads effectively. How do you scare the scariest creature that has ever existed? You can’t. So it becomes something different. It becomes about dread. It becomes about what Anne wrote about: the punishment of time. But that’s perhaps not the best subject for a horror movie in general. That’s what I had to grapple with, to make it kind of terrifying. The terror had to come from within, or the terror had to come from the ideas of these characters themselves.
	
	
		So much of that dread comes from the visual language of the film — the way it’s directed, the cinematography, the lighting. What was one of the most challenging sequences for you to shoot?	

	The big stuff is not that difficult. We were lucky enough to be at a period before CGI had taken over the world and taken over cinema. Everything that we saw in the film had to be photographed. We built that New Orleans set, and we burned it. We had cameras across the Mississippi. It probably was one of the last times when you could actually do that. 

	CGI was just in its infancy, and we had a great special effects supervisor, Rob Legato, who had just set up Digital Domain with James Cameron, but that whole movement of cinema into something that is not essentially unreal hadn’t begun yet — or at least I wasn’t aware of it.

	The most difficult scene to shoot is where Tom has that prostitute in his room, and she gradually realizes that she’s with two vampires. He puts her in a coffin, and Lestat is trying to force Louis to admit who he is. That was a difficult set of scenes to shoot. I think we went on for about eight days. That was the essence of the movie: Lestat getting Louis to embrace the monster within him.
	
		That just reminds me of one of the other deleted scenes, the ones the one at the beginning, where Lestat is sitting down and then he gets up and he’s got the bullet hole through his hand. Why did that get left on the cutting room floor?	

	Maybe there was something slightly theatrical about it that you know that didn’t deserve to stay within the film. I don’t remember why these scenes were not in the final cut. I just know that the first time I showed the movie, saying to David Geffen and to Warner about this, “Look, this film is too long and David insisted on previewing what we had shot in front of an audience. The audience watched it, said, “Oh, the film is too long.” I had already worked out how to compress certain things. But it’s I’m glad those scenes are available to people and fans of the movie to see.
	
		I want to go back to format for a second. Audiences love seeing movies in Imax, even Imax 70mm. If you were making this movie today, would you consider shooting it in Imax 70mm?	

	I spoke with Christopher Nolan last night. I was asking him about that. I’m not sure I would be able to wheel those bloody cameras around. I do like to be able to hold a camera on my shoulder, I love 35mm. I love the way you hear the film whirring through the gate. I’m not sure I’d be able to handle Imax. If I ever get to make another big studio movie, I’ll definitely look into it. I will.
	
	
		What would you say to somebody that has never seen your “Interview with the Vampire?	

	I’d say it’s a companion piece to an earlier movie I made, “The Company of Wolves.” 

	This interview has been edited and condensed.

	Watch the deleted scene below.

schema.headline: Neil Jordan on Restoring ‘Interview With the Vampire’ for 4K and Why the Film Didn’t Have Jump Scares

title: Paramount-Warner Bros. Settlement: What the Guilds, AGs and Activists Are Saying
description: After almost a year in the trenches pulling together his historic combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, David Ellison has fi
body:
After almost a year in the trenches pulling together his historic combination of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery, David Ellison has finally emerged victorious. On Monday, the Silicon Valley heir confirmed he’d reached a settlement with a group of state attorneys general, who sued to block the merger over antitrust concerns. 

	The proposed merger was met with heated opposition by activist groups, top talent like Mark Ruffalo and  whispers by Ellison’s legacy media competitors. But groups like the Hollywood labor guilds are celebrating the settlement news, as the staring contest between Ellison and the AGs caused paralysis in development and spending seemingly across the board at both companies.
	

	Here are the cheers, jeers and looming fears of the players involved in “ParaBros”: WGAThe outspoken union acknowledged that their own active litigation against the ParaBros. merger could no longer continue once the state AG’s settled, largely over the cost of duking it out in court.


	“We continue to believe the merger will cause damage to writers and the industry at large. Now that the Attorneys General have settled with Paramount, however, as a nonprofit, the WGA must contend with the reality of forging ahead alone, with no backing from government enforcers, with a complex antitrust lawsuit that would cost millions of dollars to pursue through trial. Consequently, we have also settled our lawsuit with an agreement from Paramount to prohibit writer layoffs at CBS News Broadcast for 5 years, and to pay $17.5 million to our health fund along with our attorneys’ fees in the litigation. Though we were not successful in blocking the merger, our advocacy brought more attention to the harms that this merger—and others like it—will cause. We will continue to fight the harms of industry consolidation.

	As the number of outlets to sell our work to and the corresponding diversity of programming shrinks, we need industry-wide structural separation between streamers and studios in order to promote competition in programming, like the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules once required in broadcast television. We will continue to fight for these goals.”
	

	DGAThe Directors Guild of America highlighted protections that the AG’s negotiated (read a comprehensive list of those here). 

	“We congratulate the parties on reaching an agreement that addresses a number of critical concerns related to the Paramount/WBD merger. The AG agreement contains important binding and enforceable commitments that protect theatrical film and television markets and domestic film jobs. Equally important, it brings clarity and stability to the industry during a period of decreased production. We especially thank California Attorney General Rob Bonta, and New York Attorney General Letitia James, for their leadership. We intend to continue our discussions with Paramount regarding domestic television production, with a focus on ensuring a competitive and robust marketplace that protects jobs.”

	SAG-AFTRAThe actors union underscored the power of collective bargaining. 

	“The settlement of the Attorneys General antitrust lawsuit, announced today, addresses some of our deep concerns about production levels and investment in U.S. production… We will continue to approach our relationship with Paramount with professionalism and the intention to work well together. We hope that the process of engaging with the attorneys general has impressed upon them the fact that in addition to collective bargaining, our members rely on the law to help protect our interests. These are the lowest standards that our employers must meet. All of the companies have the opportunity to exceed their legal obligations and make additional efforts to ensure that our workplaces are healthy and that employers honor our dignity.”

	Mark Ruffalo“Task” star Ruffalo is the face of celebrity dissent over the merger, engaging in an ugly back-and-forth with Paramount after promoting what the studio called “antisemitic tropes.”  

	“Gavin Newsom hands huge win to Trump and his billionaire cronies,” Ruffalo wrote simply on X, referring to California Governor Newsom.California Attorney General Rob BontaIf Ruffalo is the face of celebrity dissent, then Bonta was the final boss. Ellison’s most vocal opponent said this about his own settlement deal on Monday: 

	”Today, we have secured a settlement that resolves our antitrust concerns of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger — concerns that the merger will lower output and increase prices — by guaranteeing massive investment in domestic film production and providing enforceable guardrails to help keep cable prices competitive. Let me be clear: This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger. But we believe this settlement, which resolves our antitrust concerns in every market alleged in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and puts workers’ needs, concerns, and futures first, is the best course of action. When we get down to brass tacks, what we heard over and over from people who would be most directly and immediately impacted by the merger is that what matters most is consistent film output, domestic production, and protecting the livelihoods of workers above and below the line. As such, our settlement provides court-enforceable commitments for more films, an infusion of an additional $1.5 billion into home-grown film production, and protections for workers who are impacted by the merger. There’s no Hollywood without the people who work on and off screen to make the magic happen, and today’s settlement protects workers, jobs, and Hollywood.”Block the Merger Coalition The advocacy group formed this summer in response to the pending merger went, as predicted, scorched earth:“We vehemently oppose the agreement to allow David Ellison to take over Warner Bros. Discovery. This is a bad deal for the future of film, entertainment, independent journalism, and a strong democracy in this country. We are disappointed and angry that the interests of average Americans have been trampled to benefit oligarch billionaires.“The Ellisons and other forces arrayed against us, but that didn’t stop us and so many others from standing up. We are proud of what we accomplished, and together, our coalition will keep fighting. From the thousands of leaders in the film and entertainment industry and elected officials, to the hundreds of thousands who joined them to make their voices heard, even in the face of potential retaliation, this was a grassroots movement that proved Americans are not going to take this corruption anymore. That energy is not going away.“This isn’t the last we will hear of the Ellisons or the fallout of this merger – and it’s not the last you will hear from us. Block the Merger was never just about one merger, but about the harms of media consolidation and promoting a diversity of voices. We will continue fighting for accountability and policy reforms to break up and prevent these large conglomerates. This one battle may be over in our efforts to defend democracy, but we won’t stop fighting until we win the war.”

	More to come …

            Carrot Top's Las Vegas shows at the Luxor have been canceled through next Monday as the comedian remains hospitalized following a suspected overdose involving prescription pills ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The 61-year-old's performances through Sept. 28 have been called off while he continues receiving medical care.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we first reported Carrot Top, whose real name is Scott Thompson, took prescription pills Friday before suffering the suspected overdose.
      

            We're told the longtime Luxor headliner remains hospitalized but is awake, breathing on his own and continuing to improve.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Police were spotted at his Las Vegas home Friday afternoon ... and it's unclear when he will be back on stage.

title: Ohio Lawyer Who Tried To Shoot Ex in Public Sentenced to Nearly 25 Years in Prison
description:
Ohio Lawyer Who Tried To Shoot Ex
                          Sentenced to 24 1/2 Years in Prison
body:
Ohio Lawyer Who Tried To Shoot Ex
                          Sentenced to 24 1/2 Years in Prison
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 21, 2026
                            2:02 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The former Ohio lawyer whose attempt to shoot his ex-wife in public was foiled by his gun's safety just had the book thrown at him ... the judge sentenced him to nearly a quarter-century behind bars and used video of the attack to tear apart his defense.
      
    
            Matthew Exton was sentenced Monday for attempted murder, two counts of felonious assault, and multiple firearm charges after he was convicted earlier this month in a trial that went viral.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            The 43-year-old insisted he never intended to kill or hurt his ex-wife ... calling the charges political and arguing, "Guns don't kill people, people kill people."
      

            Judge Gary Cook wasn't buying it ... he played surveillance footage showing Exton scrambling with the weapon after it failed to fire, telling him, "You are flummoxed by the fact that it did not go off, and you're trying to fix the safety."
      
    
            The judge said that moment cemented Exton's intent.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Exton walked into a crowded Toledo restaurant in April 2025, pointed a loaded gun at his ex-wife and pulled the trigger -- but the safety was still engaged.
      
    
            A waiter tackled him before he could try again, and several patrons helped wrestle away the weapon.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Prosecutors later claimed Exton impersonated a police officer to buy a gun in 2024 ... and they also pointed to alleged death threats, an unauthorized late-night entry into the victim's home, and testimony that he bragged he could "kill anyone and get away with it."
      
    
            Exton's Ohio law license remains suspended.

title: Presley Gerber Checked Into Rehab Hours Before Suspected Overdose
description:
Presley Gerber
                          Checked Into Rehab Home Hours Before Suspected OD
body:
Presley Gerber
                          Checked Into Rehab Home Hours Before Suspected OD
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 21, 2026
                            12:10 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 21, 2026
                                12:57 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Presley Gerber checked into rehab the night before he was pronounced dead from a suspected drug overdose ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources familiar with the situation tell TMZ ... the 27-year-old model entered the Santa Monica luxury rehab facility on Saturday night ... only hours before police found him unresponsive on the property.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The facility provides treatment for people dealing with substance-abuse issues, mental-health problems, trauma, and other medical issues. 
      

            As we first reported ... several other people were living in the co-ed residence ... and the 911 call came in at 9:35 AM on Sunday for a suspected overdose.
      
    
            First responders attempted life-saving measures on Presley, but he was pronounced dead at the scene at 9:45 AM ... less than a day after he checked into the facility.  
      
    
            An autopsy has been completed, but the cause of death has been deferred.
      
    
            Presley, the only son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, started modeling as a teenager ... and in recent years he opened up about his struggles with substance abuse and mental health.

title: Late NBA Star Elgin Baylor: Family War Over Fortune Erupts In Court
description:
Late NBA Star Elgin Baylor
                          Daughter Fighting Stepmom Over His Fortune
body:
Late NBA Star Elgin Baylor
                          Daughter Fighting Stepmom Over His Fortune
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 21, 2026
                            3:30 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            NBA legend Elgin Baylor's family is fighting over his estate, years after his death ... and it's getting nasty.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Elgin's daughter, Alison Clayton, filed a petition claiming her stepmom, Elaine Baylor, is withholding information about her inheritance. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Elgin died on March 22, 2021, at 86 ... and Alison said her stepmom, who was with Elgin at the time, didn't let Alison or her brother know their dad had died, and has since refused to reveal any information about the estate. 
      

            Alison said she moved to the East Coast in 1991 but remained in contact with her dad until around 2018.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She said her stepmom knew she had a relationship with her dad for years but still decided to cut her out of the situation. 
      
    
            Elaine has yet to respond to the case.
      
    
            Elgin is in the Basketball Hall of Fame ... he was the No. 1 overall NBA draft pick in 1958 and played 14 seasons for the Lakers. He's widely considered one of the best players of all time.

body:
Carrot Top
                          Suffered Suspected OD From RX Pills
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 21, 2026
                            1:25 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Carrot Top was hospitalized following a suspected overdose from prescription pills ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            A rep for the Clark County Fire Department tells TMZ ... crews responded to the comedian's Las Vegas home around 4:20 PM Friday after receiving a call about a 61-year-old male who was "not alert."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            We're told a City of Las Vegas ambulance and a private ambulance responded. Carrot Top's condition was unknown at the scene, and he was transported to a hospital by the private ambulance.
      
    
            Sources familiar with the investigation tell TMZ ... Carrot Top took prescription medication before suffering the suspected overdose.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... the comedian, whose real name is Scott Thompson, attempted suicide Friday and was rushed to a hospital. His Friday, Saturday, and Monday night shows at the Luxor were canceled as a result.
      
    
            Carrot Top's rep told us Sunday he "remains hospitalized and under close medical care. He is now awake, breathing on his own and continuing to improve, surrounded by his family and those closest to him."
